title: Introduction and the concept of the state

questions.prompt: Which aid may you use alone in the Staatsrecht exam, according to the organisational slides?

options.text: Any law commentary you prefer
options.why: Commentaries and loose notes are not named as the sole permitted aid.

options.text: Basistexte Öffentliches Recht in the Beck-Texte im dtv edition
options.why: The lecture names that volume as the required and permitted text collection.

options.text: Printouts of all Moodle slides
options.why: Slides are for learning; the named Basistexte volume is the exam aid.

options.text: A different edition of Basistexte without checking the named Beck/dtv volume
options.why: You must use the edition the course specifies, not any similar book.

questions.explain: Think of the exam as “open book, one book only.” The course points you to a single statutory collection so everyone works from the same texts. Underlining and small sticky notes with keywords are allowed; full loose sheets are not.

questions.prompt: Which five structural principles does the syllabus link to Art. 20 I GG?

options.text: Democracy, social state, rule-of-law state, federal state, republic
options.why: The lecture lists all five as Grundprinzipien tied to Art. 20 I GG.

options.text: Democracy, rule-of-law state, and federal state only
options.why: Sozialstaat and Republik are also named in the syllabus.

options.text: Separation of powers, democracy, and human dignity
options.why: Those ideas matter elsewhere; this list is the five Art. 20 I principles from the handout.

options.text: Monarchy, federal state, and social state
options.why: Republik and Demokratie rule out monarchy as a listed principle here.

questions.explain: Art. 20 I GG is the anchor for how Germany defines itself structurally. The five words often appear together in exams: Demokratie, Sozialstaat, Rechtsstaat, Bundesstaat, Republik. Remembering all five beats knowing only the three most famous.

questions.prompt: In the abbreviation list on the slides, what do BR and BT stand for?

options.text: BR = Bundestag; BT = Bundesrat
options.why: The letters are swapped: BR is the Bundesrat, BT the Bundestag.

options.text: BR = Bundesrat; BT = Bundestag
options.why: That matches the glossary in the lecture materials.

options.text: Both mean the same federal parliament
options.why: They are two different organs with different roles in federal lawmaking.

options.text: BR = Basic Law revision; BT = budget treaty
options.why: Those expansions do not appear in the course abbreviation list.

questions.explain: Picture two rooms in Berlin: elected MPs in the Bundestag (BT) and representatives of the Länder in the Bundesrat (BR). Mixing the two abbreviations is a common slip on written tests.

questions.prompt: Which court decides EU law, and which applies the European Convention on Human Rights in the Europarat system?

options.text: EGMR for EU law; EUGH for the EMRK
options.why: The roles are the other way around in the lecture glossary.

options.text: EUGH for EU law; EGMR for the EMRK
options.why: The slides distinguish Europäischer Gerichtshof (EU) from the Strasbourg human-rights court.

options.text: Both are EU institutions with the same jurisdiction
options.why: The EMRK system is tied to the Council of Europe, not the EU court structure.

options.text: Bundesverfassungsgericht for both
options.why: The question asks about the European courts named EUGH and EGMR.

questions.explain: EU membership and Council of Europe membership overlap for Germany, but the courts are separate. EU law → Luxembourg (EUGH). Convention rights under the EMRK → EGMR in Strasbourg.

questions.prompt: How should you cite a rule in the Grundgesetz versus a rule in the Parteiengesetz (PartG)?

options.text: GG with §; PartG with Art.
options.why: The Basic Law uses Artikel; ordinary statutes use Paragraph (§).

options.text: GG with Art.; PartG with §
options.why: That is the citation style taught on the Vorbemerkungen slides.

options.text: Both always with § only
options.why: Constitutional and EU texts in this course use Art., not §.

options.text: Both always with Art. only
options.why: Federal acts like PartG are cited with § and the statute abbreviation.

questions.explain: When you see “Art. 5 GG,” that is normal. When you see party rules, you write “§ 4 Abs. 1 PartG.” Using the wrong symbol marks you as not yet reading like a jurist.

questions.prompt: In Art. 5 GG, the unit marked “(1)” is an Absatz. What are the clauses inside it that end with full stops?

options.text: Each full stop starts a new Absatz
options.why: Several Sätze can sit inside one Absatz.

options.text: Sätze (sentences) within the same Absatz
options.why: The slide labels Satz 1 and Satz 2 inside Absatz 1 of Art. 5 GG.

options.text: Always Nummern, because they are numbered ideas
options.why: Nummern are list items like “1.”; press freedom here is a Satz, not Nr. 1.

options.text: Buchstaben a), b), c)
options.why: Letter items are lit.; Art. 5 Abs. 1 uses running sentences, not a) b) c).

questions.explain: Absatz = the bracketed subsection. Satz = a sentence inside it. The lecture uses Art. 5 to show that Pressefreiheit sits in Satz 2 of Abs. 1—not in a separate Article.

questions.prompt: According to the definition slide, what is Staatsrecht mainly about?

options.text: Contracts between private companies under the BGB
options.why: That is civil law (Zivilrecht), not Staatsrecht.

options.text: How the state is organised, who acts for it, and how citizen–state relations are structured
options.why: That matches the three-part summary on the slide.

options.text: Only criminal procedure under the StPO
options.why: Criminal law is a separate field, even though it is formally public law.

options.text: Only the Grundgesetz, with no other statutes
options.why: The slide also names acts such as BWahlG, StAG, and BVerfGG.

questions.explain: Staatsrecht lives under Öffentliches Recht. It is wider than “just the GG”: elections, nationality, and the BVerfGG also belong to the picture. Civil law sits beside that box, for citizen-to-citizen relations.

questions.prompt: On the police slide, where does preventive danger prevention (Gefahrenabwehr) mainly find its legal home?

options.text: Strafrecht and the StPO
options.why: Repressive work on Straftaten ties to StPO; prevention is drawn differently.

options.text: Public law, notably the NPOG (Lower Saxony Police Act)
options.why: The flowchart links präventive Aufgaben from NPOG to Öffentliches Recht.

options.text: Private law under the BGB
options.why: Police core tasks are not framed as ordinary private-law contracts.

options.text: Only EU regulations, not Land law
options.why: The example statute on the slide is the Niedersächsisches NPOG.

questions.explain: Police work splits: chasing crimes → criminal law and StPO; stopping dangers before they become crimes → public-law Gefahrenabwehr, with NPOG as the local anchor in this course.

questions.prompt: Georg Jellinek’s Drei-Elemente-Lehre names three elements. Which set is correct?

options.text: Staatsgebiet, Staatsvolk, and originäre Staatsgewalt
options.why: All three appear on the numbered definition slide.

options.text: Democracy, Rechtsstaat, and Sozialstaat
options.why: Those are constitutional principles, not Jellinek’s three elements.

options.text: Bundestag, Bundesrat, and Bundesverfassungsgericht
options.why: Those are organs, not the territory–people–power triad.

options.text: Territory and people only; effective control is optional
options.why: The slide says missing any one element means no Staat under this concept.

questions.explain: Territory includes more than dry land (airspace, coastal belt). Staatsvolk means a durable bond, not fee-paying fans. Staatsgewalt must be original sovereign power, not borrowed from another state.

questions.prompt: Neptun-Land: an ex–oil rig 15 nautical miles off Sylt, “citizens” who pay a fee, and self-declared royal rules. Under the three-element theory on the slide, is that a Staat?

options.text: Yes, because someone calls himself king and people pay to join
options.why: Titles and fees do not replace territory, Volk, and genuine sovereign power.

options.text: No; the scenario is meant to show missing or weak elements of statehood
options.why: Aufgabe 1 asks you to apply the theory—micronation play fails the legal test.

options.text: Yes, because it lies outside the 12-mile coastal belt
options.why: Distance from shore does not create Staatsgebiet in Germany’s legal space.

options.text: Yes, once enough countries recognise it
options.why: Recognition is treated separately; the exercise tests the three elements first.

questions.explain: The lecture uses Neptun-Land as a puzzle: fun story, serious method. Ask each element in order. Payment for a “passport” is not a Staatsvolk; a rig is not a stable Staatsgebiet with originäre Gewalt.

questions.prompt: How does the lecture relate diplomatic recognition (Anerkennung) to the legal concept of a state?

options.text: Recognition and fulfilling the legal Staatsbegriff are the same thing
options.why: The slides treat recognition as a political act that can diverge from legal qualification.

options.text: Recognition is political; it does not automatically match the legal concept of statehood
options.why: You can meet or fail the concept independently of who recognises you.

options.text: Only the United Nations decides legal statehood
options.why: The UN count (193 members) is factual context, not the definition itself.

options.text: Legal statehood never matters for international law
options.why: Völkerrecht needs subjects—mainly states—with a workable Staatsbegriff.

questions.explain: Sealand on the slide is a Schein-Staat story: flags and titles entertain, but lawyers still ask about territory, people, and power. Recognition by other governments is a separate, political step.
